title: Vayakhel: the women's mirrors (Exodus 38:8)
hookLine: the washing basin is made from women's copper mirrors; Rashi says God held them most dear

lines: ONE SENTENCE IN A LONG LIST.
cards: Before glass mirrors, people looked at themselves in polished metal: a disk of copper or bronze, rubbed until it shone. In the desert, some Israelite women had mirrors like that.

Small, personal things, the kind you might not think to give to a holy building. In the middle of a long list of what Bezalel made, the Torah stops for one sentence to say where the metal for a single object came from.
The object is the washing basin. The metal came from those mirrors.

teach.h: MIRRORS OF THE WOMEN AT THE DOOR.
teach.b: The verse says Bezalel made the basin of bronze, and its stand of bronze, from the mirrors of the women who served at the door of the tent of meeting.
The basin stood between the tent and the altar, and the priests washed their hands and feet in it before they served. The Torah says nothing more about who the women were or why they gave.
Rashi fills the silence with a midrash.
When the women brought their mirrors, Moses hesitated. These were made for vanity, he thought, for looking pretty. Then God said to him: accept them.
These are dearer to Me than everything else. Why? Because of Egypt.
The midrash says that when the men came home crushed from the slave labor, these women took their mirrors, sat beside their husbands, made them laugh and look again, and kept love alive.
Families kept growing, even in slavery, and because of those mirrors, the midrash says, a people survived to leave.

So, in the midrash, the very objects Moses nearly turned away became the basin the priests washed in before they served. A mirror shows you yourself. A basin of water is where you prepare to serve someone else.
The same metal did both. And in Rashi's telling, the gift that looked least holy was the one God held dearest.

how: Rashi's midrash on the mirrors is a well-loved teaching on the portion Vayakhel, often cited to honor the women of the Exodus whose courage kept families alive in slavery.

the bronze basin where the priests washed

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: the Torah tells us who the women at the door were
the text is silent. the story of why their mirrors mattered comes from midrash, through Rashi.
in Rashi's midrash, Moses nearly turned the mirrors away
he saw them as tools of vanity. God told him to accept them.
the basin was where the priests washed before serving
their hands and feet, between the tent and the altar.

games.q: you're Moses. women bring polished mirrors, things for looking beautiful, as gifts for the holy sanctuary. what do you do?
o: hesitate: these seem made for vanity.
melt them down for the altar.
games.why: in Rashi's midrash, Moses hesitates, and God says: accept them, these are dearer to Me than everything. they became the basin.

practice: Think of something someone gave that nobody counted as important: a mother who kept the house laughing in a bad year, a friend who sent silly texts when things were dark.
Name exactly what they gave, and what it made possible later. If you pray, give thanks for them; if not, just let the gift be seen.

wordCard.voice: Vayakhel. The portion where Bezalel builds, and the women's bronze mirrors become the basin the priests wash in.

orig.note: Hebrew: mirrors, from the root ra'ah, to see; the word in Exodus 38:8.
